newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Singapore port in tough fight against rivals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Singapore port in tough fight against rivals.

text.p: Singapore is facing an increasingly tough fight against regional competitors to maintain its position as Southeast Asia's premier port, shipping experts say.
Right now, Singapore's numbers are looking very good in terms of how much cargo passes through its port, which sits at the end of the Malacca Strait, the main route between Asia and the West.
The Port of Singapore Authority (PSA) said 1.09 million containers passed through its hands last September, compared with 978,000 in September 1995.
That translates into nearly 64 million tonnes of cargo in September 1996, up from 58 million in the same month in 1995.
But competition from other Southeast Asian ports appears to be making a dent in Singapore's rate of growth.

The government's latest economic survey said Singapore's transport and communications sector grew at only 6.2 percent in the third quarter of this year after 10.7 percent growth in the first quarter and 8.5 percent in the second.
REGIONAL COMPETITORS GEAR UP TO TAKE BUSINESS BACK
Shipping experts said that decline means Singapore will have to battle hard to keep its share of the pie as neighbours rush to overhaul their ports and to take away business.
Neighbouring Malaysia is making a major effort to promote Port Klang and the experts say it has already succeeded in diverting some business away from Singapore.
Malaysian companies ship goods worth around 130 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$5.14 billion) through Singapore a year.
About a quarter of Malaysia's overseas trade passed through Singapore last year and industry sources said they estimated transhipment costs were 500 million ringgit.
This factor helped aggravate Malaysia's trade deficit -- 773.4 million ringgit in October -- and has spurred Kuala Lumpur into action to cut down transhipment through Singapore.
In November, Malaysia raised truck charges for goods to and from Singapore, effectively doubling shippers' handling charges.

The aim was to encourage Malaysian shippers to use Port Klang and the adjacent West Port, the 1.2 billion ringgit duty- free port officially launched on Malaysia's west coast earlier this year by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohammad.
Kuala Lumpur has vowed to do its utmost to turn West Port into a regional shipping hub specialising in containers and bulk grain.
INDONESIA, THAILAND JOIN THE RACE
Malaysia is not the only challenger to Singapore's domination of the region -- some 70 percent of Singapore's traffic is heading to or from other Southeast Asian ports.
Indonesia is developing Bojonegara port in western Java, with an initial investment of $700 million.
It aims to give the port the capacity to accomodate the latest generation of container ships with draughts of up to 18 metres (59 feet) and able to carry more than 6,000 containers.
Thailand is also rushing to expand port facilities at Laem Chabang, about 100 km (60 miles) southeast of Bangkok, to reduce congestion at the capital's overworked port.

A Maersk Line official told Reuters his company and other carriers had already started to use Port Klang and Thailand's Laem Chabang for containers previously moved by feeder carriers through Singapore.

Further afield, Hong Kong, Asia's biggest container port, looks set to boost its service of a vast hinterland after the British colony is returned to Chinese rule. Colombo and Taiwan will also be bigger competitors in the years ahead, the sources say.
SINGAPORE SAYS DETERMINED TO STAY AHEAD
The PSA said in a statment to Reuters that it was confident of maintaining its eminence over the long haul.
"It is good for regional ports to develop and improve their efficiency because overall connection times will be reduced as a result," it said.
"However, in the end, shipping lines will have to decide which port gives them the best value in moving goods fastest, most reliably and cost-effectively."
Nor is it standing still.
The PSA has spent Singapore $1.12 billion (US$800 million) this year, or about three times the S$381 million it spent last year, mostly to develop a new container terminal at Pasir Panjang.
That, it said, would enable Singapore to meet demand for container handling facilities well into the 21st century.
The PSA said it also planned to focus more on expanding operations outside Singapore.
The port authority told Reuters that the Dalian Container Terminal in northern China had "got off to a good start with a 17 percent growth in container traffic in the first half of this year".
The PSA started container operations at its joint venture in the Chinese port last July.
And over the coming year, PSA plans to become a corporation, a step towards privatisation, a move widely believed to be part of its bid to sustain a competitive edge.
